description: A stout perennial from a deep taproot with big, upright, oval leaves 20-40 cm long, grey and woolly when young, and a large yellow sunflower-like head 7-10 cm across on a short, leafy stem; 20-60 cm tall. It flowers from March into May in the blue oak savanna and on grassy slopes, most often on north- and east-facing ground and among rocks, where deer eat its young leaves and flowers in spring and quail and ground squirrels pick up its seed.

season_notes.winter: The first woolly grey leaves push up through the grass after the rains.
season_notes.spring: Clumps of big grey ears, with one or a few large yellow heads each, March into May.
season_notes.summer: The leaves brown and wither in June; by July nothing shows above the root.
season_notes.fall: Nothing above ground; the taproot waits for the rains.

notes: Gray mule's ears is a foothill perennial of the Sierra Nevada and Coast Range, in blue oak savanna, open woodland and grassland, usually on slopes, frequently north- or east-facing and in rocky ground. The leaves are mostly basal, broadly elliptic to ovate, 20-40 cm long, held up and out like a mule's ears and covered with a dense grey-white wool that thins with age (leaf shape ovate, 0.3 m, a grey-green); the heads are solitary or few on short stems, 7-10 cm across, a ring of bright yellow rays round a yellow disc like a small sunflower (flower shape daisy, 9 cm, 2 per plant). It is summer-dormant: the leaves appear in December-January, flowering is March-May, and the leaves dry and collapse by July, so height_by_month is zero from July to November and the June value shows the browning leaves (dead_rgb). Deer eat the tender young leaves and the flower heads; ground squirrels and quail take the seeds. habitat: north x1.4 and steep x1.2 follow its liking for the cooler slopes; the rock outcrops have no factor of their own, so the slope factors stand for them; light shade at most (0.2); rarely on disturbed ground (0.5), since the taproot plant is slow to establish.
